meta.title: Who really said "When I Wrote It, Only God and I Knew the Meaning; Now God Alone Knows"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Hegel. A floating anecdote told about at least six men since 1826 — and the 1875 writer who pinned it on Hegel called it a myth in the same sentence.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When I Wrote It, Only God and I Knew the Meaning; Now God Alone Knows'?
meta.ogDescription: A joke retold about Richter, Böhme, Fichte, Hegel, Klopstock and Browning. Quote Investigator dates it to 1826 and judges every version fictional.

answer.label: Not Hegel — an anecdote retold about at least six different men
answer.authorName: Unknown — a floating anecdote, earliest documented 1826
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · first in print 1826, about Johann Paul Friedrich Richter · attached to Hegel in 1875
answer.sourceLine: This is one of the most widely travelled jokes in intellectual history, and it was never Hegel’s. Quote Investigator’s survey ↗ finds the earliest instance in The Morning Chronicle of London on 9 August 1826, where it is told about the German writer Johann Paul Friedrich Richter, who had died the year before: “when I wrote that passage, God and I knew what it meant. It is possible that God knows it still; but as for me, I have totally forgotten.” Over the following century the same quip was reassigned to Jakob Böhme, Johann Gottlieb Fichte, Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock, Hegel and Robert Browning. The wording people quote today is closest to the Browning telling. QI’s conclusion is that each of these tales was fictional — every one of them began circulating only after the man it featured was dead.
answer.confidenceText: Every documented telling is traced; none of them is Hegel speaking. The man who first attached it to Hegel labelled it a myth in the same breath.

source.heading: Where the anecdote actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Morning Chronicle, London, 9 August 1826 — about Johann Paul Friedrich Richter (d. 1825)
John Fiske, 1875 (vol. 1, footnote on p. 120) — who called it “A myth, no doubt”
The Church Quarterly Review, July 1890, p. 319 — told about Robert Browning and his poem Sordello
Apocryphal — a migrating joke with no verifiable speaker

source.excerpt: The story is current that on being asked to explain some difficult passage written years before, the great metaphysician gave it up in despair, saying: “When I wrote that passage, there were two who understood it.—God and myself. Now, alas, God alone understands it!” A myth, no doubt, but crudely characteristic, like most myths.
trail: Quote Investigator’s article ↗ assembles the chain with full bibliographic citations: the 1826 Morning Chronicle original about Richter, an 1857 version about Jakob Böhme, Harriet Beecher Stowe pinning it on Fichte in 1869, Fiske’s Hegel footnote in 1875, the earliest Browning telling in 1890, Klopstock in 1891, Mark Twain recording the Browning version in an 1896 notebook, and G. K. Chesterton calling it “probably apocryphal” in 1903.

QI’s conclusion is the load-bearing part, and it is not a hedge: “QI hypothesizes that each of these comical tales was fictional. Each instance began to circulate only after the death of the featured individual.” A remark that only ever appears once its speaker can no longer be asked about it is the signature of an invented anecdote.
Hegel’s own Wikiquote page ↗ does not carry this line at all — not in its sourced quotations and not among its attributed ones. For a quip this famous, that absence is itself evidence.

The joke outlived its sources by becoming theatre. Rudolf Besier put it in the mouth of Browning in The Barretts of Wimpole Street (1930), and QI quotes the scene: “when that passage was written only God and Robert Browning understood it. Now, only God understands it.” A 1952 article in Modern Language Notes by W. P. Bowman recognised the line in that play and traced it back to 1827; QI then found the 1826 instance.
source.cutTag: John Fiske, Outlines of Cosmic Philosophy, 1875 — the Hegel version, with Fiske’s own verdict attached
source.excerptNote: This is the passage that attached the joke to Hegel, and it is worth reading to the end: Fiske tells the story and then calls it a myth in the same breath. The disclaimer dropped away and the anecdote kept travelling — which is how Hegel ended up credited with a line his own source said he never spoke.

source.rightsNote: Every documented telling of this anecdote is from the nineteenth century — the 1826 Morning Chronicle item, Fiske’s 1875 footnote and the 1890 Church Quarterly Review version are all long out of copyright in the United States. The joke itself is anonymous, so there is no author or estate to hold a right in it.

author.name: G. W. F. Hegel
author.heading: About G. W. F. Hegel
author.bio: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was a German philosopher and a major figure in the tradition of German idealism, whose Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) and Science of Logic (1812–1816), with lectures on the philosophy of history and on fine art published after his death from students’ notes, carried his influence across both the analytic and the continental traditions. He also acquired a reputation for near-impenetrable prose — the Phenomenology is, in Wikipedia’s words, “infamous for… its conceptual and allusive density, idiosyncratic terminology, and confusing transitions.” That reputation is the reason this anecdote found him: the joke needs a thinker whose readers are willing to believe he lost his own thread.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is not a quote with one wrong owner; it is a joke that has been hung on a succession of famously difficult writers for two hundred years. Quote Investigator documents every name below.

items.why: The Hegel version first appears in John Fiske’s Outlines of Cosmic Philosophy (1875), and Fiske presents it as hearsay he does not believe — “A myth, no doubt” — per Quote Investigator ↗. Hegel died in 1831, forty-four years earlier.

The 1826 Morning Chronicle instance is the oldest QI could find, and it features Richter, who had died in 1825. Being first in print is not the same as being true: QI judges this telling fictional too ↗, on the same posthumous-appearance grounds.

Browning died in 1889; the first Browning telling QI locates is from 1890, about his notoriously opaque poem Sordello. G. K. Chesterton, writing a Browning biography in 1903, already called the story “probably apocryphal” — see Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Jakob Böhme, Johann Gottlieb Fichte and Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock
items.why: Böhme in an 1857 New York quarterly, Fichte in an 1869 newspaper column by Harriet Beecher Stowe, Klopstock in an 1891 treatise on genius and madness. QI prints all three ↗; each man was long dead by the time his version appeared.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody can be shown to have said it. It is a two-hundred-year-old joke about unreadable prose that attaches itself to whichever difficult writer is currently in the air — and, as Quote Investigator ↗ notes, it has probably been genuinely redeployed by living wits many times since, which is how a fiction acquires the texture of a quotation.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke works because it flatters and wounds at once: it grants that a writer once had a meaning, and takes away any hope of recovering it. That is why it keeps finding new hosts. Every generation has a thinker it suspects of being deliberately impenetrable, and the anecdote is a ready-made verdict on him — which is also why it is so rarely checked.

Hegel was an unusually good target. Even admirers conceded the difficulty: Fiske, in the very footnote that spread the story, had just called Hegel “unquestionably one of the clearest, strongest, and most consecutive reasoners that the world has ever seen.” The anecdote is the complaint that praise could not quite suppress, and it travelled further than the praise did.
context.pull: A joke that only ever surfaces after its speaker has died is not a quotation. It is an obituary with a punchline.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI dates the earliest known instance to The Morning Chronicle, London, 9 August 1826, told about Johann Paul Friedrich Richter, who died in 1825.
QI quotes John Fiske’s Outlines of Cosmic Philosophy (1875), vol. 1 p. 120 footnote, giving the Hegel version and calling it "A myth, no doubt, but crudely characteristic, like most myths."
QI gives the earliest Browning telling as The Church Quarterly Review, July 1890, p. 319: "When I wrote it, only God and I knew; now God alone knows!"
QI concludes: "QI hypothesizes that each of these comical tales was fictional. Each instance began to circulate only after the death of the featured individual."
Hegel’s Wikiquote page does not contain this quotation in any section.
